messages.subject: Re: In fieldIndex NAs produced by integer overflow
messages.subject_clean: In fieldIndex NAs produced by integer overflow
messages.body_plain:
Eric,

I got your point. To remove soil, we are using vegetation
indices that recognize what is green in the image, right. During the senescence
time, the majority of the pixels are brown and they will be removed by
fieldMask(). Then, when you use this mask to select pixels and calculate the CHM
you will get the error. That’s happening because you removed all pixels and
there is no information to compare with the soil base.

My suggestion is (1) to not use the mask to calculate CHM, or (2)
to use the same mask made with the flight with greater canopy (flowering time)
for all flights. In other words, you must adjust the pipeline using one flight
from Flowering time, get and save the mask to use it during the removing soil
step before calculating the CHM. In some cases, the flights will have some soil
area, but I don’t think this is a problem here.

Hope it helps… Let us know if this strategy works.

All the best,

Filipe

messages.body_plain:
Hi Filipe,

Thanks for looking into this!

I forgot to include how I create my CHM mask, but I use a DEM and a DTM to create the CHM and then a height threshold for the mask, no orthomosaic. The problem arises after I use the DEM-derived mask to extract the VI data from the orthomosaic rasters, specifically VARI and BGI for both the RGB sensor and multispectral sensor. The issue also occurs regardless of phenological stage, leaf-out/flowering/harvested/senescence. It's just strange that for the exact same shapefile ID, all other bands, VI's, and structural data will be presented but for these few VI's the results are NA or inf.

This is my CHM masking code but I don't believe this is causing the problem.

DEM <- stack("rasters/p4p/DSM/210227_UVT_p4p_DSM.tif")
DTM.R <- resample(DTM.dormant, DEM)
CHM <- DEM-DTM.R
CHM.plant <- CHM
CHM.plant[CHM.plant<.05] <- NA
CHM.mask <- CHM
CHM.mask[CHM.mask<.05] <- 1
CHM.mask[CHM.mask<1] <- 0
CHM.mask[CHM.mask>1] <- 0
plot(CHM.mask)

Thanks,

Eric

messages.subject: image set normalization
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm new to using FIELDimageR but have been getting useful results from my set of RGB images. Thanks Filipe for making the software available to the research community and providing a forum for support!

While my results are useful, I've been looking for ways to improve them. My images are a time-series set of field plots taken every 2 weeks. I've noticed some unexpected variation between some sets and have considered that this variation could be due to differences between lighting conditions when the images were captured. Some of the mosaics appear clear and bright while others appear to have some (cloud?) shading.

Is it recommended to normalize sets of images to minimize differences in brightness prior to FIELDimageR processing? If so, can you recommend any specific tools or protocols to use/follow?

Thanks,
Brian

I wanted to follow up with another possibility for improving my results. I've noticed that when using the default fieldMask() parameters to remove soil from my images, some leaves with a more yellow color are also being masked. I should also mention that I'm working with loamy soil that can appear very light when dry.

I've looked through the fieldMask() documentation, but am not sure what parameters would be best to modify. I also know that it may be asking a bit much of the software to differentiate between soil and yellow vegetation, but am willing to try any suggestions to see if an improvement is possible.

Thanks again,
Brian

messages.subject: Re: FIELDimageR: image set normalization
messages.body_plain:
Hi Brian,

This is true and we always have differences between lighting conditions. I normalized each RGB image using the mean and standard deviation (some author using mean and standard deviation between all the images too):

# Normalized values in RGB --------------------------------------------------------
library(terra)
RGB<- terra::rast("YOUR_IMAGE.tif")
RGB <- subset(RGB, 1:3)
norf <- function(x, ...) {
  v <- values(x)
  v <- (v - mean(v)) / sd(v)
  setValues(x, (255 / (max(v)-min(v))) * (v-min(v)))
}

# `sapp` loops over layers
RGB.normalized <- sapp(RGB, norf)

The reference paper is (Page 6):

Xu, D.; Pu, Y.; Guo, X. A Semi-Automated Method to Extract Green and Non-Photosynthetic Vegetation Cover from RGB Images in Mixed Grasslands. Sensors 2020, 20, 6870. https://doi.org/10.3390/s20236870

Cheers,

Alexandre

messages.subject: Using Shapefile to crop Images
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to use the shapefile to crop out each image. I have 9 rows and 4 columns, so a total of 36 plots. I would like to have 36 resulting cropped images of each plot for further analysis in Python. I have tried the function previously given:

plot_clip <- function(ortho, shape){ +  plot_raster <- list() +  for (i in 1:nrow(shape)) { +  cat("plot_", i, " ") +  p <- shape[i,] +  plot_raster[[i]] <- crop(x = ortho, y = extent(p)) +  plot_raster[[i]] <- mask(plot_raster[[i]], p) +  names(plot_raster)[i] <- shape$plot[i] +  } +  return(plot_raster) + }

then
> rasterbyplots <- plot_clip(EX1.RemSoil, EX1.Shape)

but I get the following error:
Error in 1:nrow(shape) : argument of length 0

Have I missed a step somewhere?

messages.subject: Re: Using Shapefile to crop Images
messages.body_plain:
Hi William,

Maybe you are using the full output from fieldMask(), which is a list.

This function requires a single raster per time.

Try to use EX1.RemSoil$mask (binary output) or EX1.RemSoil$newMosaic (RGB output) instead of only EX1.RemSoil.

Let us know if it works ... ok

All the best,
Filipe

messages.subject: image cropping based on spatial positioning
messages.subject_clean: image cropping based on spatial positioning
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a situation that is a bit different from the tutorial examples. The field I'm working on has several thousand ~1m x 1m research plots. This makes any FIELDimageR functions that require manual selection, like fieldShape(), difficult to perform precisely due to the small image window and inability to zoom in rstudio.

My current workaround is to use an image editor (gimp) to rotate and crop my raw images while zoomed in to precisely select the field corners. These rotated/cropped images can then be processed automatically using the fieldShape() extent = TRUE option. (instructs fieldShape() to use the entire image and skip manual corner selection) This works well for basic processing like canopy percentage. However, gimp is not geotiff-aware, so it does not export spatial information after rotating/cropping, crippling it's usefulness.

Moving forward, I'm considering pre-processing steps similar to those above. Avoiding manual selections in FIELDimageR while retaining spatial information in the rotated/cropped TIFs is the goal. Ideally I'd automate as much of the processing as possible for consistency (and speed!) between the time-series images I have. This seems feasible, but I have very limited experience with geotiff files and am not sure if there is a way to get spatial coordinates from field corners in an image and if those coordinates can be used for cropping. If anyone has experience doing this, I'd like to hear more about your process.

Thanks,
Brian

Filipe

messages.subject: Re: tuning soil masking
messages.body_plain:
Hi Brian,

Thanks for asking us. The best way is to choose different vegetation indices and try to find the best thresholding value to make your segmentation between plants and soil. Please, check this example using the index “BGI”: https://github.com/OpenDroneMap/FIELDimageR#P6. Normally, plotting the histogram helps to find the best clipping point (between pics of histogram bars)

Image<- stack("Image.tif")

 Image.BGI<- fieldIndex(mosaic = Image, index = c("BGI"))

 dev.off()

hist(Image.BGI$BGI) # Image segmentation start from 0.7 (soil and plants)

 EX1.BGI<- fieldMask(mosaic = EX1.Rotated, Red = 1, Green = 2, Blue = 3,

                   index = "BGI", cropValue = 0.7, cropAbove = T)

 #Check if: cropValue=0.8 or cropValue=0.6 works better.

Also, there are some explanation about image segmentation in this tutorial of how to count seeds from images using FIELDimagR. Besides being different objects (seeds vs. plants) the idea to segment the background is the same You can use this to understand the concepts. Here is the link https://filipematias23.github.io/FIELDimageR-Workshop-12/#example-03

Hope it helps,

Filipe

all cases is possible to obtain a thresholding value by some criteria
decision like Otsu’s multilevel thresholding method (MOM). The
autothresholdr package does it, but index values must be discretized.
For example for an NDVI raster:

land_ndvi_F <- round(land_ndvi*100,0)

# Percentile Otsu’s multilevel thresholding method (MOM)
MOM<-auto_thresh(
int_arr=values(land_ndvi_F),
method="Percentile",
ignore_black = FALSE,
ignore_white = FALSE,
ignore_na = TRUE
)
MOM
[1] 33
or 0.33 in real NDVI data scale.

Best wishes,
Alexandre
